title: Chebyshev Sequence Design: Clearing √5 Denominators
content: The sequence cosThreeFifthsSeq is engineered so that d_n = 5^n · 2cos(n·arccos(3/5)) is always an integer, despite cos(arccos(3/5)) = 3/5 being rational with denominator 5. Multiplying by 5^n clears all denominators from the Chebyshev evaluation: the recurrence d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} - 25d_n has integer coefficients 6 = 2·(6/5)·5 and 25 = 5². This parallels nivenSeq in OQ02, where multiplying by 3^n cleared the 1/3 denominator from arccos(1/3).
mathContext: For $\cos\theta = 3/5$, the Chebyshev recurrence $2\cos((n{+}2)\theta) = 2\cos\theta \cdot 2\cos((n{+}1)\theta) - 2\cos(n\theta)$ gives $5^{n+2} \cdot 2\cos((n{+}2)\theta) = 6 \cdot [5^{n+1} \cdot 2\cos((n{+}1)\theta)] - 25 \cdot [5^n \cdot 2\cos(n\theta)]$. The key cancellation: $5^{n+2} \cdot 2\cos\theta = 5^{n+2} \cdot 6/5 = 6 \cdot 5^{n+1}$, so all factors of 5 absorb into integer coefficients. The resulting sequence $d_n \in \mathbb{Z}$ satisfies $d_0 = 2$, $d_1 = 6$, $d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} - 25d_n$.

title: Mod-5 Divisibility: Parallel to OQ02's Mod-3 Argument
content: The proof that 5 ∤ cosThreeFifthsSeq n exactly mirrors the proof that 3 ∤ nivenSeq n in OQ02. The recurrence d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} − 25d_n reduces mod 5 to d_{n+2} ≡ d_{n+1} (mod 5) — since 6 ≡ 1 and 25 ≡ 0. So the non-divisibility propagates: from 5 ∤ d_n and 5 ∤ d_{n+1}, we derive 5 ∤ d_{n+2}. The base: d_0 = 2, d_1 = 6 — neither divisible by 5.
mathContext: If $5 \mid d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} - 25d_n$, then since $5 \mid 25d_n$ we get $5 \mid 6d_{n+1}$. Since $\gcd(5, 6) = 1$ ($5$ is prime, $5 \nmid 6$), we conclude $5 \mid d_{n+1}$, contradicting the inductive hypothesis. Formally: `Prime.dvd_or_dvd : p prime, p | ab → p | a ∨ p | b`, applied to $6 \cdot d_{n+1}$ with $p = 5$. The induction maintains the pair $(\lnot 5 \mid d_n, \lnot 5 \mid d_{n+1})$ simultaneously.

title: Half-Angle Identity: 2·arccos(1/√5) = arccos(-3/5)
content: The proof computes cos(2·arccos(1/√5)) = 2·(1/√5)² − 1 = 2/5 − 1 = −3/5, then uses Real.arccos_cos to identify the angle: since 2·arccos(1/√5) ∈ [0, π] (because arccos(1/√5) ≤ π/2, which holds since 1/√5 ≥ 0), and its cosine equals −3/5, it must equal arccos(−3/5). The key Mathlib fact: arccos_le_pi_div_two says arccos x ≤ π/2 iff x ≥ 0.
mathContext: Double-angle formula: $\cos(2\theta) = 2\cos^2\theta - 1$. With $\theta = \arccos(1/\sqrt{5})$: $\cos(2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})) = 2 \cdot (1/\sqrt{5})^2 - 1 = 2/5 - 1 = -3/5$. Range check: $0 \leq 2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5}) \leq \pi$ follows from $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5}) \in [0, \pi/2]$ (since $1/\sqrt{5} \geq 0$). By injectivity of $\cos$ on $[0,\pi]$ and `Real.arccos_cos`, we conclude $2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5}) = \arccos(-3/5)$.

title: Chain of Irrational Angles: 3/5 → 1/√5 → -1/√5
content: The irrationality propagates through a three-step chain. First, arccos(3/5)/π ∉ ℚ (proved via cosThreeFifthsSeq). Second, if arccos(1/√5)/π = r ∈ ℚ, then arccos(3/5)/π = 1 − 2r ∈ ℚ (using 2·arccos(1/√5) = π − arccos(3/5)), contradiction. Third, if arccos(-1/√5)/π = r ∈ ℚ, then arccos(1/√5)/π = 1 − r ∈ ℚ (using arccos(-x) = π − arccos(x)), contradiction. Each step is a simple rational arithmetic consequence.
mathContext:
Three-step irrationality chain: $\arccos(3/5)/\pi 
otin \mathbb{Q}$ (base) $\Rightarrow$ $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})/\pi 
otin \mathbb{Q}$ $\Rightarrow$ $\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})/\pi 
otin \mathbb{Q}$. The steps use: (1) $2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5}) + \arccos(3/5) = \pi$, so if $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})/\pi = r$ then $\arccos(3/5)/\pi = 1 - 2r \in \mathbb{Q}$, contradiction; (2) $\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5}) = \pi - \arccos(1/\sqrt{5})$ by `arccos_neg`, so if $\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})/\pi = r$ then $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})/\pi = 1 - r \in \mathbb{Q}$, contradiction.

title: From Angle Irrationality to Nonzero Dehn Invariant
content: The transition from angle irrationality to a nonzero Dehn invariant follows a two-step argument. First, dodAngle_infinite_order shows that the angle class [arccos(-1/√5)] has infinite order in ℝ/πℤ: if n·[arccos(-1/√5)] = 0 for some n ≠ 0, that would imply arccos(-1/√5)/π = m/n ∈ ℚ, contradicting dodAngle_irrational. Second, tmul_infinite_order_ne_zero (the flatness axiom from OQ02OQ02) converts infinite order of the angle class into nonvanishing of the tensor product: r ⊗ [θ] ≠ 0 whenever r > 0 and [θ] has infinite order.
mathContext: The Dehn invariant group is $\mathbb{R} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} (\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z})$. The edge term for the dodecahedron is $\text{edgeTerm}(30a, \theta_{\text{dod}}) = 30a \otimes [\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})]$. Nonvanishing uses: (1) $[\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})]$ has infinite order $\Leftrightarrow$ $\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})/\pi \notin \mathbb{Q}$; (2) $r > 0$ and $[\theta]$ infinite order $\Rightarrow$ $r \otimes [\theta] \neq 0$ (from flatness: $\mathbb{R}$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}$, so the map $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}$ induces injections on tensor products).

title: Icosahedron: Deferred Chebyshev Argument in ℤ[√5]
content: The icosahedron's dihedral angle arccos(-√5/3) ≈ 138.19° requires an irrationality proof over the quadratic ring ℤ[√5], which is deferred as an axiom. The argument would parallel the dodecahedron proof: define a sequence e_n satisfying a recurrence with coefficients in ℤ[√5] (or clear √5 denominators by doubling the sequence), prove non-divisibility by 3 using the prime structure of ℤ[√5], and conclude that arccos(-√5/3)/π ∉ ℚ. The remaining structure — deriving infinite order of [arccos(-√5/3)] and then the nonzero edge term — is fully proved conditional on this axiom.
mathContext: For $\cos\theta = -\sqrt{5}/3$, the Chebyshev recurrence gives $2\cos((n{+}1)\theta) = 2\cos\theta \cdot 2\cos(n\theta) - 2\cos((n{-}1)\theta) = (-2\sqrt{5}/3) \cdot 2\cos(n\theta) - 2\cos((n{-}1)\theta)$. Setting $e_n = 3^n \cdot (\sqrt{5})^{n \bmod 2} \cdot 2\cos(n\theta)$ would give an integer sequence, but the argument requires verifying that $3$ does not divide $e_n$ for all $n$, which needs ideal-theoretic reasoning in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{5}]$ (the prime $(3) = \mathfrak{p}\bar{\mathfrak{p}}$ splits since $\sqrt{5} \not\equiv 0 \pmod{3}$).

title: Complete Platonic Solid Classification by Dehn Invariant
content: The theorem cube_isolated_dehn_invariant packages the complete 5-solid classification into a single conjunction. The cube (12 edges, π/2 dihedral) has D = 0; all other Platonic solids have D ≠ 0. The tetrahedron and octahedron results come from OQ02OQ02; the dodecahedron is new in this file; the icosahedron uses the axiomatized angle irrationality. The classification has an immediate geometric consequence: no scissors-congruence exists between the cube and any other Platonic solid. This extends Hilbert's original 1900 question (cube vs tetrahedron) to the complete Platonic family.
mathContext: Euler characteristic $V - E + F = 2$ for each solid. Dihedral angles: Cube ($\pi/2$), Tetrahedron ($\arccos(1/3)$), Octahedron ($\arccos(-1/3)$), Dodecahedron ($\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})$), Icosahedron ($\arccos(-\sqrt{5}/3)$). Dehn invariant $D(P) = \sum_e \ell(e) \otimes [\theta(e)] \in \mathbb{R} \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} (\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z})$. Since $\pi/2 = \frac{1}{2}\pi$ is a rational multiple of $\pi$, $[\pi/2] = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z}$, so $D(\text{cube}) = 0$. All other dihedral angles are irrational multiples of $\pi$, giving nonzero Dehn invariants and ruling out scissors congruence with the cube.
